pharmacistLine.active: Whatever it is, tell the pharmacist about your breast-cancer medicine every time — even for things off the supermarket shelf.
pharmacistLine.pending: Whatever it is, tell the pharmacist about your breast-cancer medicine (tamoxifen, expected soon) every time — even for things off the supermarket shelf.

noclash.label: No known clash
noclash.lead: Nothing known against it alongside your treatment.

unknown.label: Not on the list
unknown.lead: Not on my list — ask the pharmacist before taking it.

unknownWhy: This notebook only knows the things already written into it. Anything else is a question for the pharmacist, not for an app.

medicines.name: Paroxetine
medicines.why: Blocks the enzyme tamoxifen needs in order to work.

medicines.name: Fluoxetine
medicines.why: Blocks the enzyme tamoxifen needs in order to work.

medicines.name: Bupropion
medicines.why: Blocks the enzyme tamoxifen needs in order to work.

medicines.name: Diphenhydramine
medicines.why: Interferes with the enzyme tamoxifen depends on. It hides in several night-time remedies.

medicines.name: St John's Wort
medicines.why: Interferes with tamoxifen.

medicines.name: Black cohosh
medicines.why: Interferes with tamoxifen.

medicines.name: Soy isoflavone supplements
medicines.why: Oestrogen-like activity — and fermented soy is one of your migraine triggers.

medicines.name: “Bioidentical” compounded hormones
medicines.why: Not regulated, and they contain hormones.

medicines.name: HRT of any kind
medicines.why: Only ever a decision for your breast team.

medicines.name: Duloxetine
medicines.why: Strong effect on the tamoxifen enzyme.

medicines.name: Sertraline
medicines.why: Moderate effect on that enzyme.

medicines.name: Chlorphenamine
medicines.why: May affect that enzyme.

medicines.name: Hydroxyzine
medicines.why: May affect that enzyme.

medicines.name: Cimetidine
medicines.why: Affects that enzyme.

medicines.name: Escitalopram / citalopram
medicines.why: Often considered suitable alongside tamoxifen — but confirm with the pharmacist.

medicines.name: Ibuprofen and other anti-inflammatories
medicines.why: Can push blood pressure up and clash with candesartan. Counts towards your painkiller days.

medicines.name: Pseudoephedrine decongestants
medicines.why: Raise blood pressure.

medicines.name: Vitamin E and high-dose antioxidant supplements
medicines.why: Ask the oncologist, especially around radiotherapy.

medicines.name: Melatonin
medicines.why: Check with the pharmacist alongside your other medicines.

medicines.name: Candesartan
medicines.why: Your daily preventer — doing double duty for migraine and blood pressure.

medicines.name: Sumatriptan
medicines.why: Your migraine rescue. The Today screen counts the days it's used.

medicines.name: Paracetamol
medicines.why: No known clash. Counts towards your painkiller days.

medicines.name: Magnesium
medicines.why: Part of your migraine routine, no known clash.

medicines.name: Riboflavin (vitamin B2)
medicines.why: Part of your migraine routine, no known clash.

medicines.name: Coenzyme Q10
medicines.why: Part of your migraine routine. Ask the oncologist whether to pause it during radiotherapy week.

medicines.name: Codeine and co-codamol
medicines.why: Two problems: codeine relies on the same enzyme as tamoxifen, and opioids cause medication-overuse headache faster than anything — from 10 days a month. Counts towards your painkiller days.

medicines.name: Migraleve
medicines.why: Contains codeine and buclizine, an antihistamine. Both are worth checking against tamoxifen, and the codeine puts it in the 10-days-a-month bracket for overuse headache.

medicines.name: Syndol
medicines.why: Contains codeine and an antihistamine — same cautions as Migraleve.

medicines.name: Aspirin
medicines.why: Can push blood pressure up and irritate the stomach. Counts towards your painkiller days.

medicines.name: Naproxen
medicines.why: An anti-inflammatory like ibuprofen — can raise blood pressure and clashes with candesartan. Counts towards your painkiller days.

medicines.name: Ibuprofen gel and other rub-on anti-inflammatories
medicines.why: Rubbed on rather than swallowed, so far less effect on blood pressure than tablets. Often the better option for a sore joint — worth asking the pharmacist.

medicines.name: Other triptans
medicines.why: Same family as your sumatriptan. Rizatriptan in particular needs care alongside some blood-pressure medicines. Any triptan counts at 10 days a month for overuse headache.

medicines.name: Caffeine tablets
medicines.why: Raises blood pressure, and a caffeine spike-then-crash is its own migraine trigger.

medicines.name: Domperidone
medicines.why: Broken down by a different liver route from tamoxifen, so it's often the anti-sickness option raised first for people on tamoxifen. Still a prescription decision — ask.

medicines.name: Metoclopramide
medicines.why: A common anti-sickness drug for migraine, but it blocks the enzyme tamoxifen needs. Worth flagging before anyone prescribes it.

medicines.name: Cyclizine
medicines.why: Also affects the tamoxifen enzyme. Mention the tamoxifen before accepting it.

medicines.name: Prochlorperazine
medicines.why: Often given for migraine sickness. Its effect on the tamoxifen enzyme isn't clear-cut, so have the pharmacist check.

medicines.name: Ondansetron
medicines.why: Usually prescribed by the hospital. Fine to ask how it sits with tamoxifen.

medicines.name: Night Nurse
medicines.why: Contains promethazine — a sedating antihistamine that interferes with the tamoxifen enzyme. The night-time cold remedies are the ones to watch.

medicines.name: Day Nurse and Lemsip Max
medicines.why: Most contain a decongestant (phenylephrine or pseudoephedrine) which raises blood pressure, plus paracetamol that counts towards your painkiller days. Plain paracetamol is usually the simpler choice.

medicines.name: Promethazine
medicines.why: A sedating antihistamine that affects the tamoxifen enzyme. Sold for both allergy and sleep.

medicines.name: Cough medicines
medicines.why: Some contain sedating antihistamines or decongestants. Read the ingredients out to the pharmacist.

medicines.name: Throat lozenges and sprays
medicines.why: Usually straightforward, but a few contain anaesthetics or antibiotics — worth a quick check.

medicines.name: Cetirizine
medicines.why: Barely processed by the liver, so it's one of the antihistamines usually considered suitable alongside tamoxifen. Still confirm with the pharmacist.

medicines.name: Fexofenadine
medicines.why: Like cetirizine, hardly touched by the liver — usually among the suitable options. Confirm before starting.

medicines.name: Loratadine
medicines.why: Partly broken down by the same enzyme as tamoxifen, so cetirizine or fexofenadine may be suggested instead. Ask.

medicines.name: Nytol Herbal and valerian
medicines.why: Different from ordinary Nytol — usually valerian rather than an antihistamine — but herbal sleep remedies still interact unpredictably. Check before starting.

medicines.name: Omeprazole and lansoprazole
medicines.why: Common indigestion tablets. Ask the pharmacist to check them against tamoxifen when you start.

medicines.name: Gaviscon, Rennie and simple antacids
medicines.why: Generally uncomplicated, but they can affect how other tablets are absorbed — leave a gap and check.

medicines.name: Peppermint oil capsules
medicines.why: Usually straightforward. Worth a mention when you get them.

medicines.name: Laxatives
medicines.why: Mostly uncomplicated, but some slow or speed how your other tablets are absorbed. Say what else you take.

medicines.name: Anti-diarrhoea tablets
medicines.why: Ask the pharmacist, especially alongside your other medicines.

medicines.name: Sage supplements
medicines.why: Sold everywhere for hot flushes, but sage acts like a plant oestrogen — best avoided with breast cancer. Cooking with sage is a different matter and isn't the issue.

medicines.name: Turmeric and curcumin supplements
medicines.why: Supplement doses interfere with how tamoxifen is broken down, so the capsules are out. The pinch you cook with is a different matter entirely.

medicines.name: Dong quai
medicines.why: Acts like an oestrogen and has been shown to encourage growth in hormone-receptor-positive breast cancer cells in the laboratory.

medicines.name: Ginseng
medicines.why: Has plant-oestrogen effects — best avoided with a hormone-sensitive cancer.

medicines.name: Wild yam
medicines.why: Marketed as a natural hormone alternative, which is precisely the reason to avoid it.

medicines.name: Flaxseed and linseed supplements
medicines.why: Has weak oestrogen-like activity and the studies conflict. Sprinkling some on porridge is different from a concentrated supplement — ask your team which you mean.

medicines.name: Evening primrose oil
medicines.why: Commonly sold for menopause with little evidence behind it. Check before starting.

medicines.name: Menopause multivitamins
medicines.why: These blends often contain soy, red clover or other plant oestrogens. Take the box to the pharmacist and have the ingredients read properly — the label rarely makes it obvious.

medicines.name: Ashwagandha and maca
medicines.why: Popular and not clearly a problem, but the evidence alongside tamoxifen is thin. Ask before starting.

medicines.name: Ginkgo biloba
medicines.why: Studied in women on hormone treatment for breast cancer, but it also thins the blood. Check first.

medicines.name: Echinacea, milk thistle and other herbal remedies
medicines.why: Herbal products interact in ways that pharmacy computer systems often miss. Look for the THR mark and always ask.

medicines.name: CBD oil
medicines.why: Affects several liver enzymes, including ones involved in breaking down tamoxifen. Ask before using it.

medicines.name: Vitamin D
medicines.why: One of the few supplements with clear guidance behind it, and bone health matters more than usual on tamoxifen before the menopause. Worth asking your GP whether you should be taking it.

medicines.name: Calcium
medicines.why: Same reasoning as vitamin D — relevant to bone strength. A question for your GP rather than something to start alone.

medicines.name: Omega-3 and fish oil
medicines.why: Generally regarded as low-risk, but it thins the blood a little. Mention it before any procedure.

medicines.name: Iron tablets
medicines.why: Only worth taking if a blood test says you need it. Iron also stops other tablets absorbing properly if taken together.

medicines.name: Multivitamins
medicines.why: Usually fine, but check the label for soy, red clover or high-dose antioxidants — they hide in blends.

medicines.name: Probiotics
medicines.why: Generally low-risk. Worth mentioning to your team anyway.

medicines.name: Thrush treatments
medicines.why: Fluconazole taken by mouth affects liver enzymes, so it's worth checking against tamoxifen. Creams and pessaries are a smaller question than tablets.

medicines.name: Vaginal moisturisers and lubricants
medicines.why: Non-hormonal moisturisers and lubricants are the recommended first step for dryness, and you don't need anyone's permission to use them.

medicines.name: Vaginal oestrogen
medicines.why: A prescription decision that has to involve your breast team — but unlike people on other hormone treatments, it isn't automatically ruled out for you. Worth raising if dryness becomes a problem.

medicines.name: Unperfumed moisturiser for radiotherapy skin
medicines.why: During radiotherapy, use an unperfumed moisturiser that's free from SLS (sodium lauryl sulphate) — many say so on the label. Not immediately before a session, and never on broken skin.

medicines.name: Aloe vera and after-sun on treated skin
medicines.why: Ask the radiotherapy team before putting anything new on treated skin — they have their own list.

medicines.name: Sun cream
medicines.why: Sensible generally, and treated skin stays sun-sensitive for a long time afterwards. Keep the treated area covered or well protected.

medicines.name: Turkey tail mushroom
medicines.why: The best-researched of the medicinal mushrooms — PSK, an extract of it, has been used alongside chemotherapy in Japan since 1980, and a trial is currently running in ER-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer. Promising rather than proven. Tell your oncology team before starting.

medicines.name: Reishi mushroom
medicines.why: Genuinely mixed evidence, and worth understanding why. One laboratory study found reishi extract encouraged growth of ER-positive breast cancer cells through oestrogen-like activity; another found it suppressed growth. Given your cancer is strongly oestrogen-driven, this one needs your oncologist's view rather than a guess.

medicines.name: Lion's mane mushroom
medicines.why: Often described as hormone-neutral, but it contains daidzein and genistein — the same isoflavones found in soy. Worth raising specifically because of that.

medicines.name: Maitake mushroom
medicines.why: Studied in a small breast cancer trial for immune effects. Low-risk in the studies so far, but small and short. Ask before starting.

medicines.name: Shiitake, chaga and cordyceps extracts
medicines.why: As concentrated extracts these are a different question from eating mushrooms, which is fine and may even be protective. Extracts warrant a check with your team.

medicines.name: Medicinal mushroom blends
medicines.why: Blends often include reishi, which is the one with an oestrogen-like signal in ER-positive cells. Take the tub to your team and let them read the ingredients.

food.intro: Nothing complicated. Steady fuel keeps the threshold higher, and that is most of the job.

sections.title: Steady fuel
lines: Eat within an hour of waking.
Try not to go more than 4 hours without food.
A small bedtime snack helps if mornings are bad.
Protein with every meal.
Slow-release carbs — wholegrains, beans, nuts — over sugary spikes.

sections.title: Worth avoiding
lines: Soy sauce, miso and fermented soy — a migraine trigger, and soy is best kept low anyway.
Keep caffeine steady rather than up-and-down.
Alcohol is a common trigger for both migraine and flushes.

sections.title: Flush-friendly
lines: Notice whether hot drinks or spicy food set flushes off.
Cold water and layers help.

sections.title: Drink through the day
lines: Dehydration is a quiet headache trigger — especially around hospital visits.

moh.title: Why the number matters
moh.text: Taking painkillers on too many days in a month can, over time, start causing headaches of its own — the headache comes back as each dose wears off, so it looks like the pain is worsening when the pattern is really the treatment. The usual thresholds are 10 days a month or more for triptans like sumatriptan, and 15 days a month or more for ordinary painkillers such as paracetamol or ibuprofen. Counting the days is the whole point of this card: it turns a vague impression into a number your GP can act on.

nudges.fasting: Long gaps without food have shown up a few times this week. A small bedtime snack, and eating within an hour of waking, often helps.
nudges.backup: Worth saving a backup — Settings → Save a backup.

painkillerCard.green: Below the level linked to medication-overuse headache.
painkillerCard.amber: Getting close to the level that can cause extra headaches.
painkillerCard.red: This level can itself cause headaches — worth telling your GP this number.

bp.overTarget: Above the home target — worth mentioning to your GP.
bp.severe: A reading this high needs prompt advice — see Urgent symptoms.

foodLookup.blurb: Type anything you're about to eat or drink. Be warned: most food is fine, and the trigger lists you'll find online are far less reliable than they look.
foodLookup.honesty: Apart from soy and alcohol, the evidence that any particular food triggers migraine is weak — studies keep coming out inconclusive. What matters far more for you is eating regularly. Don't cut things out on the strength of a list; cut things out only if you notice them yourself.

watch.label: Often blamed — evidence is weak
watch.lead: Commonly reported, but the studies don't back it up.

steady.label: Keep it steady
steady.lead: It's the change that causes trouble, not the thing itself.

check.label: Worth a word
check.lead: Worth mentioning, or going easy on.

unknown.label: Nothing known against it
unknown.lead: Not on my list — and most food isn't. Eat it if you fancy it.

foodLookup.unknownWhy: This notebook only flags the few things that genuinely matter. Everything else is just food. If you notice something setting you off, mark it as yours and it'll remember.
foodLookup.markedLabel: You've marked this as one of yours.

items.name: Soy and fermented soy
items.why: Two separate reasons: soy has oestrogen-like activity, which is best kept low with breast cancer, and fermented soy is high in tyramine — one of the triggers you already know about.

items.name: Alcohol
items.why: Linked to breast-cancer recurrence, and one of the most reliably reported triggers for both migraine and hot flushes. Red wine and beer are the usual culprits.

items.name: Caffeine
items.why: Not off-limits — but keep the amount the same each day. A sudden drop is a well-recognised migraine trigger, so a skipped morning coffee can cost you. If you want to cut down, drop by about a quarter a week rather than stopping.

items.name: Aged cheese
items.why: One of the most commonly blamed foods, but the studies are inconclusive. Only worth avoiding if you've actually noticed it yourself.

items.name: Cured and processed meat
items.why: The nitrates get blamed. Evidence is thin for migraine — though processed meat is worth keeping modest for general health anyway.

items.name: Yeast extract
items.why: High in tyramine and often listed as a trigger, but the evidence is weak. Notice rather than assume.

items.name: Smoked and pickled fish
items.why: Another tyramine-rich one that appears on every list and holds up poorly in studies.

items.name: Chocolate
items.why: Very commonly blamed — but there's a catch. Craving chocolate is often an early sign an attack has already started, so it gets blamed for something it didn't cause.

items.name: MSG and flavour enhancers
items.why: Frequently reported, poorly supported by evidence.

items.name: Artificial sweeteners
items.why: Aspartame in particular gets blamed. Evidence is mixed at best.

items.name: Citrus fruit
items.why: On most trigger lists, with very little behind it.

items.name: Protein foods
items.why: Protein at every meal steadies blood sugar, which is the single most useful thing you can do — given a day without food is what started this run.

items.name: Slow-release carbohydrates
items.why: Releases energy slowly instead of spiking and crashing. Better than anything sugary.

items.name: Water
items.why: Dehydration is a quiet headache trigger, and it creeps up on hospital days. Keep a bottle with you.

items.name: A bedtime snack
items.why: The overnight gap is the longest you go without food, which is why headaches so often arrive first thing. Something small before bed is the fix worth trying.

items.name: Sugary food on an empty stomach
items.why: Not banned — but a sugar spike on an empty stomach is followed by a crash, and the crash is the bit that triggers headaches. Better alongside some protein.

items.name: Hot drinks
items.why: A common flush trigger. Not a reason to give up tea — just worth noticing whether it's yours.

items.name: Spicy food
items.why: Another common flush trigger. Notice, don't assume.

items.name: Milk and yoghurt
items.why: Useful for bone strength, which matters more than usual on tamoxifen before the menopause. Plain dairy isn't the same question as strongly aged cheese.

items.name: Calcium-rich foods
items.why: Tamoxifen can thin the bones in women who haven't been through the menopause, so calcium in food is quietly important.

items.name: Oily fish
items.why: Good general choice, and useful for bone and heart health.

items.name: Vegetables and fruit
items.why: No catch here. Plenty of it, in whatever form you'll actually eat.

items.name: High-fibre foods
items.why: Worth knowing: painkillers — especially codeine — bung you up. Fibre and fluids help more than another tablet.

items.name: Eggs
items.why: Quick protein, which is exactly what a long gap without food needs.

items.name: Toast, cereal and simple breakfasts
items.why: The point is eating something within an hour of waking, not eating something impressive. Toast counts.

items.name: Ready meals and convenience food
items.why: On a bad day, eating something easy beats cooking something ideal and beats eating nothing by a mile. This is not the week for standards.

items.name: Herbal and decaf drinks
items.why: Fine, and a useful way to keep fluids up without moving your caffeine total around. Avoid sage tea specifically.

items.name: Sage tea
items.why: Sold for hot flushes, but sage acts like a plant oestrogen — one to leave. Sage in cooking is a different thing and isn't the issue.

items.name: Liquorice
items.why: Real liquorice in any quantity can push blood pressure up, which matters for you more than most.

items.name: Salt
items.why: Worth going easy on, purely because of the blood pressure.

items.name: Grapefruit
items.why: Interferes with how the liver handles a lot of medicines. Worth mentioning to the pharmacist given everything you take.

items.name: Energy drinks
items.why: A big caffeine and sugar spike, then a crash — both ends of that are migraine triggers, and the caffeine lifts blood pressure.

radiotherapy.intro: Most breast radiotherapy in the UK is now five sessions over one week. Here's what tends to happen, so less of it comes as a surprise.

sections.title: Your skin, and the bit nobody warns you about
lines: A skin reaction usually starts around 10 days after treatment begins — so often after you've finished.
It typically gets worse for about two weeks after the last session, then settles. That is expected, not a sign something has gone wrong.
The skin goes pink or darker, feels warm, and gets dry or tight — like a sun reaction.

sections.title: Looking after the skin
lines: Wash normally with a mild soap or shower gel, and pat dry rather than rub.
Use an unperfumed moisturiser that's free from SLS (sodium lauryl sulphate) — most say so on the label.
Moisturise often, but not right before a session, and never on broken skin.
Carry on with your usual deodorant unless the armpit gets sore — then leave that side alone until treatment finishes.
Loose cotton next to the skin. Skip underwired and tight bras for the week.
Ask the team before putting anything new on the treated area — they have their own list.

sections.title: Tiredness
lines: Radiotherapy tiredness builds through the week and can carry on for weeks afterwards.
It stacks on top of the tiredness you already have, so expect the total to be worse rather than the same.
Short walks help more than they sound like they will. Complete rest tends to make it worse.

sections.title: Protecting the week from a migraine
lines: Five days of appointments means disrupted routine, disrupted meals and less sleep — three of your reliable triggers at once.
Plan food for those days in advance rather than deciding when you get there.
Take water and something to eat to every appointment; waiting times are unpredictable.
Keep your caffeine at its usual level. A skipped morning coffee on a hospital day is a classic way to bring an attack on.
Keep your wake-up time the same, even on the days you feel wrecked.

sections.title: Worth asking before you start
lines: Whether to pause the CoQ10 for the treatment week.
Which moisturiser they'd like you to use.
What to do if the skin breaks or gets very sore.
Whether your appointment times can be grouped to suit your day.

suggestions.intro: Things that might help. The first list you can simply try. The rest are questions worth putting to the right person — tap to save any of them into Ask something.

items.text: Eat something within an hour of waking
items.why: The overnight gap is the longest you go without food, which is why headaches so often arrive first thing.

items.text: A small snack before bed
items.why: The other end of the same gap. Worth trying if mornings are the worst part.

items.text: Protein with every meal
items.why: Steadies blood sugar. A day without food is what started this run, so this one matters more than it sounds.

items.text: Keep your wake-up time the same, even on bad days
items.why: Migraine responds to routine. A lie-in can set off an attack as reliably as a short night.

items.text: Keep caffeine at the same level each day
items.why: It's the change that triggers, not the coffee. A skipped morning cup on a hospital day is a classic way to bring one on.

items.text: Carry water and a snack to every appointment
items.why: Waiting times are unpredictable, and both dehydration and a missed meal are triggers.

items.text: Layers, a fan, and cold water for flushes
items.why: Unglamorous, and the first thing every guideline recommends.

items.text: Non-hormonal vaginal moisturiser or lubricant if you need it
items.why: The recommended first step for dryness. You don't need anyone's permission, and it's sold in any pharmacy.

groups.title: Worth asking your GP
groups.blurb: Each of these came out of the research. Save them and they'll be waiting when you get an appointment.

items.text: How many days a month am I taking painkillers, and is it too many?
items.why: Above 10 days a month for sumatriptan, or 15 for paracetamol and ibuprofen, painkillers can start causing headaches themselves. The app counts the days for you.

items.text: Is my blood pressure actually at target?
items.why: It decides whether sumatriptan is safe for you — triptans aren't used when blood pressure is uncontrolled. The home target is below 135/85.

items.text: Is there room to increase my candesartan?
items.why: You're on the standard target dose for migraine prevention. If you're still getting frequent headaches, there may be headroom — simpler than adding another medicine.

items.text: Would escitalopram or venlafaxine suit me? I've read they can help migraine and hot flushes at the same time.
items.why: From the Women's Health Concern factsheet on migraine and HRT, for women who can't take oestrogen. Both are compatible with tamoxifen. Escitalopram may suit you better because venlafaxine can raise blood pressure.

items.text: Should I be taking vitamin D, and do I need calcium?
items.why: The two supplements with clear guidance behind them. Bone strength matters more than usual on tamoxifen before the menopause.

items.text: Would a greater occipital nerve block be worth trying?
items.why: An injection at the back of the head, available on the NHS, that helps around two-thirds of people with frequent headaches. Guidance says to consider it earlier when medication options are limited — which describes you.

items.text: Should I have a bone density (DEXA) scan?
items.why: Routinely offered for a different breast-cancer medicine, not usually for tamoxifen — but tamoxifen can thin the bones in women who haven't been through the menopause, and you came off HRT suddenly as well.

items.text: Should I pause the CoQ10 during radiotherapy week?
items.why: It's an antioxidant, and there's a theoretical question about antioxidants during radiotherapy. Radiotherapy is usually only one week, so pausing may cost you very little.

items.text: Which moisturiser would you like me to use on the treated skin?
items.why: Most teams have their own preference. Generally an unperfumed one that's free from SLS.

items.text: Has my contraception been discussed since the diagnosis?
items.why: Tamoxifen must not be taken during pregnancy, and hormonal contraception isn't the right choice alongside it. Easy to overlook among everything else.

items.text: Does the breast unit run a group for hot flushes?
items.why: A UK trial of nurse-led group CBT cut how much hot flushes bothered women by nearly half, with sleep and mood improving too. Worth asking whether yours offers it.

items.text: Can you check everything I take against tamoxifen?
items.why: Worth doing once, properly, with every box in front of them — including anything bought off a supermarket shelf.

items.text: Which hayfever or allergy tablet suits me best?
items.why: Cetirizine and fexofenadine are barely processed by the liver, so they're usually the ones suggested alongside tamoxifen.

items.text: Is there a gel rather than tablets for aches?
items.why: Rubbed-on anti-inflammatories have far less effect on blood pressure than swallowed ones.

suggestions.tryNote: Nothing in this list is a substitute for your own team's advice — it's the ordinary, low-risk stuff that tends to get forgotten.

noclashNote: This means it isn't known to interfere with your treatment — not that it's proven to work. Most natural products have never had a large trial, because nobody funds one for something that grows on a log. Absence of evidence isn't evidence of absence, but it isn't proof either. Still worth telling your team you take it.
